newsitem.title: GERMANY: Institutes say Germany to miss Maastricht targets.
newsitem.headline: Institutes say Germany to miss Maastricht targets.

text.p: Germany will fail to meet the strict debt and deficit criteria for economic and monetary union in 1997 despite a stronger economy, the country's six leading economic research institutes said in a semi-annual report issued Tuesday.
The institutes said Germany's 1997 public deficit would likely be 3.5 percent of economic output, above the 3.0 percent reference value specified in the Maastricht Treaty.
"The reference values for the deficit criterion and the debt criterion set in the Maastricht Treaty will not be reached in 1997, based on data available today," the report said.

Maastricht specifies that EMU participants' overall outstanding debt should be below 60 percent of gross domestic product, but the treaty gives considerable leeway on how the criteria will be applied.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel immediately took issue with the report and said he would ensure Germany meets the tough criteria for European monetary union.
"The federal government will continue its strict consolidation course," Waigel said. "It will create the conditions so that the 1997 deficit lies below 3 percent of gross domestic product."
1997 is the key year for deciding what countries will participate in EMU at the scheduled start in January 1999.
Waigel has projected Germany's deficit will be 2.5 percent of GDP in 1997, comfortably below the Maastricht target.

Waigel and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer have been among the most vocal advocates that the criteria be strictly interpreted to ensure the new Euro currency will remain at least as stable as the German mark.

The institutes said German GDP was likely to grow 1.5 percent in 1996, rising to 2.5 percent growth in 1997. The 1996 projection was up from a forecast of 0.75 percent growth made by the same institutes six months ago.

The report said Germany's total public sector deficit will probably fall by 17 billion marks to 127 billion marks in 1997 as the rise in government spending is slowed and taxpayer withholdings are increased, but the deficit would still be 3.5 percent of GDP.
Despite the expected overshoot in the budget deficit, the institutes still expected EMU to happen.

In their semi-annual report, which serves as a reference for the government and does not necessarily influence policy, the institutes said hitting the targets at the beginning of European monetary union was less important than continued stability after the start.

"We assume that EMU will happen," chief economist Werner Schatz of the Kiel-based Institute of the World Economy (IfW), one of the six, told a news conference. "The (Maastricht) treaty allows for the possibility that the criteria will not be precisely met.
"What's important is a commitment to stability, with sanctions, for the period after the start," Schatz said.
